paragraphs.heading: Planets beyond the Sun
paragraphs.text: An exoplanet, also called an extrasolar planet, is a planet outside our Solar System. The first confirmed one was found in 1992 circling a pulsar, and the first around a main-sequence star came in 1995. In 2016 it was realised that a possible sign of one had already been recorded in 1917. As of 5 November 2026 there were 6,464 confirmed exoplanets in 4,849 planetary systems.

paragraphs.heading: How they are found
paragraphs.text: Astronomers have many ways to detect exoplanets. Two methods, transit photometry and Doppler spectroscopy, have found the most. Both are biased, though: they spot large planets close to their star far more easily. For NASA's Exoplanet Archive, a planet counts as confirmed when separate observing techniques show features that nothing but a planet could explain, or through analytical techniques.

paragraphs.heading: A huge range of worlds
paragraphs.text: The lightest exoplanet known, Draugr, has about twice the mass of the Moon. The heaviest on the NASA Exoplanet Archive, HR 2562 b, is about 30 times Jupiter's mass, and by some definitions it may really be a brown dwarf. Orbits take anywhere from less than an hour to thousands of years. The nearest exoplanets circle Proxima Centauri, the closest star to the Sun, 4.2 light-years from Earth, and there is evidence for planets in other galaxies.

paragraphs.heading: Planet or brown dwarf
paragraphs.text: Where a planet ends and a brown dwarf begins is debated. One rule uses the mass limit for fusing deuterium, currently put at 13 Jupiter masses for objects of solar metallicity: objects that orbit stars below it are planets, and objects above it are brown dwarfs. But that cut-off has no precise physical meaning, and some objects lighter than it can fuse deuterium. Another idea is to sort by how they formed: giant planets are widely thought to grow by core accretion, while brown dwarfs form like stars, from gas clouds collapsing under gravity.

paragraphs.heading: The search for life
paragraphs.text: Finding exoplanets has boosted interest in looking for life beyond Earth. Planets in a star's habitable zone, where liquid water could exist on the surface, get special attention. About one in five Sun-like stars may have an Earth-sized planet in that zone. With 200 billion stars in the Milky Way, that suggests 11 billion such planets, or 40 billion if red dwarfs are counted. The James Webb Space Telescope, working with other observatories, is expected to tell us more about their make-up and conditions.

paragraphs.heading: Planets with no star
paragraphs.text: Some planets are not part of any planetary system; these are called rogue planets. The Milky Way may hold billions of them. They are usually treated as a separate category from planets, especially the gas giants, which are often counted as sub-brown dwarfs.
